claims.text: An integrated EML, rapid-DSC, and in-situ high-energy X-ray imaging approach can accurately and efficiently determine melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family.
Arc-melted and homogenized bulk HEAs with equimolar or near-equimolar compositions are suitable starting materials for the approach.
EML can induce containerless melting while rapid DSC and high-energy X-ray radiography simultaneously track thermal and volumetric changes.
A high-purity inert atmosphere can prevent oxidation during these measurements.
Optimizing heating and cooling rates for each HEA can minimize thermal gradients and supercooling.
The proposed measurements can achieve temperature errors below 1%.
The proposed DSC measurements can resolve enthalpy changes with uncertainty within 3%.
Transient melt-solid interface characteristics connect macroscopic calorimetric signatures to atomic-scale melting dynamics.
Containerless processing minimizes contamination and extrinsic nucleation sites.
High-speed calorimetry can precisely measure the heat flow associated with an HEA phase change.
Concurrent X-ray imaging can directly provide volume-change and density data during solid-to-liquid transformation.
The combined measurements enable estimation of entropy of fusion and other liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The integrated method will measure melting temperature, latent heat, entropy of fusion, and volume expansion simultaneously.
Enthalpy and entropy measurements will have errors of approximately ±3%.
Systematic deviations between calorimetric and volumetric measurements will not exceed 2–3%.
The method is applicable across a wide range of multi-principal-element alloys and will yield a consistent thermodynamic description of the HEA family.
Conventional crucible-based DSC exhibits substantial scatter because of container reactions, overheating gradients, and oxidation.
The approach is most effective when the levitated liquid is homogeneous and well-defined.
Rapid oxidation, magnetic interference, or extreme viscosity can place an alloy outside the method's optimal applicability range.
High heating rates may perturb equilibrium melting behavior, and surface tension in levitated melts may alter measured volume changes.
